keywords: Socks / stockings pedūlia, pedūlium n. pl. Ancient words Neo-Latin usage pedūlia, pedūlium n. pl. — socks in modern active Latin; Mir’s transcribed routine explicitly uses the word in this sense. The classical adjective is pedūlis, pedūle , “for the feet.” impilia, impilium n. pl. — felt foot-coverings; another modern lexical choice for socks. ūdō, ūdōnis m. (plural ūdōnēs ) — felt or fur sock; ancient, historically more specific. tībiālia, tībiālium n. pl. — leg coverings, gaiters or stockings; fasciae pedūlēs — foot-wraps. Pedūlia indue. — Put your socks on. Pedūlia exue. — Take your socks off.

keywords: Cap / hat / container cap distinction pilleus, pilleī m. pilleus, pilleī m. — close-fitting cap or hat, originally of felt; Traupman uses it for “cap” (pp. 116 and 286). Applied here to modern caps without claiming every modern shape was ancient. Pilleum indue. — Put on your cap. Ubi est pilleus tuus? — Where is your cap? A container’s cap or lid is operculum, operculī n. , not this headwear noun. See the lid / blender entry . The alternative single-l spelling pīleus has a different vowel-quantity convention; this entry follows Traupman’s pilleus . Sources & evidence Lewis & Short: pilleus · Morgan–Owens: hat: cap · Traupman: Conversational Latin, fourth edition

keywords: fābulae fabulae Theodōrus et pater Button up / zip / inside out / back to front clausūra tractilis Neo-Latin Working descriptions globulīs stringere — button up (Traupman 116); lexicon-notes-01 gives it with a direct object as globulōs stringere . Tunica inversa est; iterum indue. — The shirt is inside out; put it on again. (composed example). Clausūram tractilem sūrsum trahe. — Pull the zip up. (composed example).
